lead: Vermont has faced major floods in recent summers, along with long winters. DryFlare helps owners from Burlington to Montpelier and Rutland get water out and dry.
risk: summer flash floods, frozen pipes and ice dams
risk_short: flash floods, frozen pipes, ice dams
why: In July 2023, heavy rain flooded downtown Montpelier, Barre and towns across central Vermont. In July 2024, floods hit many of the same areas again. Tropical Storm Irene in 2011 washed out roads and homes across the state. Vermont's steep valleys send water into towns fast.

Old farmhouses and village homes are common, with almost a quarter built before 1940. They often have stone foundations and little insulation. Winters bring frozen pipes and ice dams, and ski homes sit empty for long stretches. New Hampshire and New York share these risks.
image_alt: Cutting a sheet of drywall with a utility knife
image_caption: Rebuilding after Vermont's river floods starts with cutting and hanging new drywall.
tips: Buy flood insurance even if you are not in a mapped zone; many 2023 losses were outside them.
Use a remote temperature alarm in second homes.
Clear snow from roof edges after big storms.
insurance: Very few Vermont homes damaged in 2023 had flood insurance. Flood is a separate policy and takes 30 days to start.

faq.q: How do I clean up after a Vermont river flood?
faq.a: Wait until officials say it is safe. Wear boots and gloves; floodwater carries sewage and fuel. Take photos, then remove mud, wet drywall and insulation. Start drying within 48 hours to stop mold.

licensing: Vermont's Office of Professional Regulation registers residential contractors. Plumbers and electricians need state licenses.
licensing_faq: Residential contractors in Vermont register with the Office of Professional Regulation. Plumbing and electrical work need state licenses.
